chapter: The McShann band on the road and at the Savoy
title: The stolen music, Lucky Enois and the earlier lost trunk
summary: The band's music was stolen from the auditorium; Ramey recalls a previous loss in Baltimore blamed on Lucky Enois.

story.theme_name: Getting paid: wages, tips and leaving over money
story.community_name: Getting paid: wages, scale and the pay envelope

blocks.x: And when I came to pick it up, there wasn't nothing there and the guys evidently had gotten on a train and gone. Now, it could have been somebody there in the place, because nobody liked it.
No, well, Jay said that two guys came in and saw the caretaker at the auditorium and told them they were to pick up McShann's things and went off with a trunk full of music.
That might have been two of the guys in the band.
Two of the guys in the band?
Might have been. And I still got my ideas of who they might have been, but, now, you think -- once before, when we had 'Lucky' Ennis as a guitar player, --

-- in charge of getting the luggage home, and the band -- we had gone back into New York City and was at the Woodside Hotel, when this guy came in and he said, man, all the music was stolen down in Baltimore. We had just finished that theater in Baltimore.
And I had to get on a train and go back down there,
and the stuff was still sitting in the back at that theatre, where he had never sent it off to the railroad station. And it was shortly after that -- now, this was in late '42.
Lucky Enos, he was supposed to be in charge of the handling of the --
Yeah, he was supposed to put the music on -- yeah, I got you.

Yeah, he was supposed to have taken it down there and put it on the railroad train. And had it shipped into New York. And evidently he was out balling some chick or something and they locked up the theater, so he came on home and said, the music -- I don't know where the music is. So I had to get on a train and go back down there, and got it.

But, anyway, McShann -- I mean, they -- for a long time they kept writing me and saying, well, what did you do to the music? Now, I was still in Kansas City. I was working at the new Reno club, out on Independence, with Oliver Todd and some other guys.

And I finally convinced them, I said, well, if I had the music, it had to be around here because I got no other place to go. So they finally got up off me. Then I did have a chance to talk with McShann and he was convinced that I
wouldn't do it no way. No, well, I mean, if you -- I mean, anybody that would take that music, you would have thought, would have used it.
Yeah. The (unintelligible) there had to sell by copies, but --
